relevance_reason: This paper describes the clinical phenotype of 20 infants with late-onset Pompe disease diagnosed through newborn screening.

findings.statement: Huggins et al. (2022) systematically evaluated 20 infants aged 6 to 21 months with LOPD diagnosed by newborn screening. None of the infants had evidence of cardiomyopathy or cardiac rhythm disturbances. CK, AST, and ALT were elevated in 8 patients (40%), and Glc4 was elevated in 2 (10%). All patients showed postural and kinematic concerns. Three patients (17%) scored below the 10th percentile on the Alberta Infant Motor Scale. Speech-language assessments were normal in all patients, and 9 (45%) had mild feeding or swallowing abnormalities. The authors concluded that phenotype varied widely and that careful physical therapy evaluation was needed to detect subtle musculoskeletal signs of early muscle involvement.
quotes: Twenty infants ages 6-21 months with LOPD diagnosed by NBS underwent systematic clinical evaluation at Duke University including cardiac imaging, biomarker testing, physical therapy evaluation, and speech-language pathology evaluation.

None of the patients had evidence of cardiomyopathy or cardiac rhythm disturbances. Biomarker testing showed an increase in CK, AST, and ALT in 8 patients (40%) and increase in Glc4 in two patients (10%). All patients demonstrated postural and kinematic concerns.
Speech-language pathology assessments were normal in all patients and mild feeding/swallowing abnormalities were noted in nine patients (45%).

phenotypes.text: motor score below 10th percentile on AIMS

findings.statement: In the 20 infants with LOPD identified by newborn screening, Huggins et al. (2022) found 4 who were homozygous for the IVS1 splice site variant c.-32-13T>G in the GAA gene. Fourteen were compound heterozygous for this variant, and 2 did not carry it.
quotes: Of the 20 infants, four were homozygous for the "late-onset" IVS1 splice site variant c.-32-13 T > G, fourteen were compound heterozygous, and two did not have any copies of this variant.

variants.as_reported: IVS1 splice site variant c.-32-13 T > G
IVS1 splice site variant c.-32-13 T > G

findings.statement: Huggins et al. (2022) studied children with LOPD diagnosed through newborn screening. Because of the high variability they found, they recommended careful physical therapy evaluation and close monitoring for symptom progression.
quotes: Careful physical therapy evaluation is necessary to monitor for subtle musculoskeletal signs that may reflect early muscle involvement. Patients should be monitored closely for symptom progression.

relevance_reason: Cohort study that characterizes tongue weakness and atrophy in patients with late-onset Pompe disease and compares them with other myopathies. It adds to the clinical features and diagnosis sections.

findings.statement: Jones et al. (2021) assessed tongue structure and function in 10 treatment-naive patients with LOPD. They compared them with 30 patients with other acquired or hereditary myopathies and 30 controls with neuropathy, using manual and quantitative muscle testing and tongue ultrasound. Compared with the neuropathic controls, the LOPD patients had significantly different tongue strength, qualitative appearance, echointensity, and thickness. The authors concluded that tongue involvement in LOPD consists of weakness and sonographic abnormalities suggestive of fibrofatty replacement and atrophy.
quotes: we assessed tongue structure and function in 70 subjects, including 10 with LOPD naive to treatment, 30 with other acquired/hereditary myopathy, and 30 controls with neuropathy
Differences in tongue strength, qualitative appearance, echointensity, and thickness between LOPD subjects and neuropathic controls were statistically significant.
These findings provide additional evidence for tongue involvement in LOPD characterized by weakness and sonographic abnormalities suggestive of fibrofatty replacement and atrophy.

phenotypes.text: increased tongue echointensity suggestive of fibrofatty replacement

findings.statement: Jones et al. (2021) found significantly lower quantitative tongue strength and significantly reduced tongue thickness on ultrasound in LOPD patients than in patients with other acquired or hereditary myopathies. They suggested that finding quantitative tongue weakness and/or atrophy may help distinguish LOPD from other myopathies. They also suggested that ultrasound is an effective point-of-care method for quantitative assessment of the tongue muscles.
quotes: Greater tongue involvement was observed in LOPD subjects compared to those with other acquired/hereditary myopathies, based on statistically significant decreases in quantitative tongue strength and sonographic muscle thickness.
Findings of quantitative tongue weakness and/or atrophy may aid differentiation of LOPD from other acquired/hereditary myopathies.

relevance_reason: A study of CNS involvement in children with Pompe disease. It includes 2 children with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) who had normal white matter on brain MRI and high developmental scores, compared with children who had infantile Pompe disease (IPD).

findings.statement: Korlimarla et al. (2020) assessed CNS involvement using brain MRI and developmental assessments in 14 children aged 6 to 18 years with Pompe disease on enzyme replacement therapy. Twelve had infantile Pompe disease and 2 had late-onset Pompe disease. The 2 children with late-onset Pompe disease had no white matter hyperintense foci and had high scores on most developmental assessments. In contrast, 10 of the 12 children with infantile disease had mild to severe white matter hyperintense foci.
quotes: The study included 14 children (ages 6-18 years) with infantile Pompe disease (IPD) (n = 12) or late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) (n = 2) receiving enzyme replacement therapy.
The 2 children with LOPD had no WM hyperintense foci, and high scores on most developmental assessments.
Mild to severe WM hyperintense foci were seen in 10/12 children with IPD (median age 10.6 years) with total FS scores ranging from 2 to 23.

phenotypes.text: white matter hyperintense foci on brain MRI

relevance_reason: Describes four clinically diagnosed patients with late-onset Pompe disease, compound heterozygous for the common GAA c.-32-13T>G variant, whose symptoms began in the first 2 years of life. Includes clinical course, GAA variants and response to enzyme replacement therapy.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) reviewed the records of 84 patients with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) carrying the c.-32-13T>G variant who were followed at Duke University Medical Center. Four patients (4.8%; 2 males and 2 females) were diagnosed clinically and had early-onset symptoms. All 4 were compound heterozygous for c.-32-13T>G and a second pathogenic variant. Symptom onset ranged from 10 days to 20 months and age at diagnosis from 10 to 26 months; median age at starting ERT was 23.5 months. The most common early features were delayed motor milestones with characteristic patterns of posture and movement (4/4), feeding difficulty (2/4) and sleep apnea (2/4). Cardiac involvement was absent.
quotes: Four patients out of 84 (4.8%) with LOPD and the c.-32–13 T > G variant, two males and two females, were diagnosed clinically and identified with early-onset symptoms. All were compound heterozygous for the c.-32–13 T > G variant and a second pathogenic variant (Table 1).

The most common symptoms of early disease onset were delayed achievement of motor milestones with characteristic patterns of posture and movement reflecting weakness typical of Pompe disease (4/4), feeding difficulty (2/4) and sleep apnea (2/4).
The lack of cardiac involvement in these patients was a likely significant contributor to the diagnostic delay.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) reported a Caucasian boy (patient 1) who presented at 5 months with delayed motor development, feeding and swallowing difficulty, easy fatigability, and snoring with likely apneic episodes. CK, ALT and AST were elevated. Muscle biopsy at 9 months showed PAS-positive vacuoles. GAA activity in fibroblasts was 4.35% of normal. At 15 months he had generalized hypotonia, head lag, myopathic facies and hypertrophied calves. EMG showed myotonic discharges, barium swallow showed penetration and aspiration, and polysomnography showed obstructive and central apneas. ECG and echocardiography were normal. He later developed coxa valga, mild ptosis and progressive thoracolumbar scoliosis that needed surgery at 12 years.
quotes: A 5-month-old Caucasian male presented with delayed motor development and feeding difficulties. Workup revealed elevated CK, ALT and AST levels.
He had generalized hypotonia, head lag when pulled to sit, myopathic facies, and hypertrophied calf muscles (Table 2). EMG showed profuse myotonic discharges consistent with Pompe disease.
Physical examination revealed mild ptosis of the left eye and increasing scoliosis. Progressive thoracolumbar scoliosis required surgery at age 12 years.

findings.statement: In patient 1, a Caucasian boy with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) sequenced GAA and found the c.-32-13T>G splice variant together with c.525delT (p.Glu176Argfs*45).
quotes: Sequencing of the GAA gene revealed c.-32–13 T > G- and c.525delT (p.Glu176Argfs*45) variants.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) described a Caucasian girl (patient 2), one of fraternal twins, who presented on day 10 of life with poor feeding, lethargy and vomiting. By 2 months she had breathing difficulty and sleep apneic episodes, and she also had hypotonia and developmental delay. Muscle biopsy at 14 months showed PAS-positive glycogen vacuoles, and blood GAA activity was low. She had failure to thrive, myopathic facies, scapular winging and neck flexor weakness, and walked at 17 months. Later problems included dysphagia needing a gastrostomy tube, gastroesophageal reflux, urinary retention, constipation, hypernasal voice and recurrent suspected aspiration pneumonia. Echocardiography and ECG were normal.
quotes: A Caucasian female, one of fraternal twins, was born at term and presented at day 10 of life with concerns of poor feeding, lethargy and vomiting. At age 2 months, she developed breathing difficulty, especially in the supine position with apneic episodes during sleep.

On clinical examination, there was failure to thrive with weight less than 5th percentile for age, height between 10th and 25th percentile and head circumference closer to 50th percentile. She had myopathic facies, scapular winging and neck flexor weakness.
She also complained of urinary retention and chronic constipation. Parents reported increased hypernasality of voice, new onset snoring and sleep disturbances/apnea.

findings.statement: In patient 2, a Caucasian girl with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.1827delC by molecular testing.
quotes: Molecular testing revealed c.-32–13 T > G and c.1827delC pathogenic variants in the GAA gene.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) described a Caucasian boy (patient 3) who could not sit unsupported or hold his head upright at 6 months. At 12 months he had an unsteady wide-based gait and frequent falls. At 23 months he had a weak cry, truncal hypotonia, proximal weakness, lordosis, scapular winging, scoliosis, a positive Gowers sign, and elevated CK, AST and ALT. Muscle biopsy showed PAS-positive glycogen storage. Later he developed mild ptosis, tongue weakness, scoliosis with a 40-degree Cobb angle, pectus excavatum, cramping, vomiting and diarrhea. His pulmonary function tests, ECG and echocardiography were normal.
quotes: He had difficulty sitting unsupported and holding head upright at 6 months, unsteady wide-based gait and frequent falls at 12 months, and tired easily compared to his peers (Table 1).

On initial evaluation by a neurologist at age 23 months, he was noted to have a soft voice with a weak cry, truncal hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, prominent lordosis, scapular winging, and scoliosis.
Additionally, he had mild ptosis, lingual muscle weakness and terminal neck flexor weakness. There was scapular winging and scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 40° for which a back brace was prescribed.

findings.statement: In patient 3, a Caucasian boy with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.2501_2502delCA (p.T834fs).
quotes: He was heterozygous for the c.-32–13 T > G and c.2501_2502delCA (p.T834 fs) variants in the GAA gene.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) reported a Caucasian girl (patient 4) born preterm at 36 weeks who needed brief CPAP for apnea and bradycardia. Her motor milestones were delayed: she stood unsupported at 20 months and walked at 22 months. She had proximal weakness with a positive Gowers sign and a waddling gait, and spinal muscular atrophy testing was negative. Blood GAA activity was low and she was diagnosed at 26 months. She also had lumbar lordosis, winged scapulae, leg pain, snoring, apneic pauses and mild reversible obstructive airway disease. Cardiology evaluations were normal.
quotes: She sat unsupported at 6 months, crawled at 12 months, stood unsupported at 20 months, and began walking without support at 22 months.
She was referred by her PCP to a neuromuscular specialist where she was noted to have proximal muscle weakness evident by positive Gowers sign and waddling gait.
She had lumbar lordosis and bilateral winged scapulae. She had pronation of the feet bilaterally.

findings.statement: In patient 4, a Caucasian girl with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.118C>T by mutation analysis.
quotes: Mutation analysis identified her GAA variants as c.-32–13 T > G and C.118C > T (Table 1).

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) noted that the second (non-IVS1) GAA variants in their 4 early-onset patients were nonsense or frameshift variants. However, c.525delT and c.1827delC were each found in 12 other patients in their LOPD cohort, all with adult-onset disease. The authors suggested that these genotype combinations are not enough to cause the early-onset phenotype. In patients 1 and 4, whose ACE genotypes were available, the unfavorable D/D genotype was absent. The authors proposed that other genetic and epigenetic modifiers might be involved.
quotes: Two of these variants, namely the c.525delT and c.1827delC, were present in 12 patients each (totally 24/83; 28.9%) in our LOPD cohort, all of who had disease-onset in adulthood, suggesting that the presence of these particular non-IVS/IVS1 genotype combinations are insufficient to cause the early-onset phenotype.
Patients 1 and 4, whose ACE genotypes were available, did not have the unfavorable D/D alleles eliminating this as a likely reason for early onset.

findings.statement: Herbert et al. (2019) found that all 4 early-onset LOPD patients improved on enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with alglucosidase alfa, but their gross motor function stayed below age level. All had residual weakness, including ptosis, lordosis, scoliosis, scapular winging, and trunk and limb weakness. Patient 1 had only partial improvement even at 40 mg/kg/week. Antibody titers stayed low in the 3 patients tested, and the authors suggested that patients with early onset have more rapid and severe progression.
quotes: Despite ERT, all had residual muscle weakness in the form of ptosis, lumbar lordosis, scoliosis, scapular winging, trunk and limb weakness, gait deviations, decreased function for age on standardized gross motor assessments, swallowing difficulty, oropharyngeal dysphagia, and gastrointestinal and genitourinary involvement in childhood.
The persistent muscle weakness in all four patients here, despite an ERT dose of 40 mg/kg/week in patient 1, underscores the importance of timely treatment.
It is important to note that antibody titers remained low in the three out of four patients in whom titers were tested

relevance_reason: Post-hoc analysis of cardiovascular findings in 87 adults with late-onset Pompe disease in a randomized ERT trial; characterizes cardiac phenotype and ERT response.

findings.statement: Forsha et al. (2011) evaluated baseline ECGs and echocardiograms in 87 patients with late-onset Pompe disease (median age 44 years, 51% male, 94% Caucasian; median disease duration 15 years) enrolled in a randomized trial. Overall, 46% had 1 or more ECG or echocardiographic abnormalities: the most common ECG findings were left ventricular hypertrophy (12%) and short PR interval (10%, 90-120 ms); 7% had decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (41-54%), and 5% had elevated left ventricular mass index on echocardiogram, all in the mild range. Other findings included bundle branch block (4%), atrial enlargement (4%), and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (2 patients).
quotes: At baseline, a short PR interval was present in 10%, 7% had decreased left ventricular systolic function, and 5% had elevated left ventricular mass on echocardiogram (all in mild range).
Overall, 46% of patients had one or more of the ECG or echocardiographic abnormalities listed in Table 2 at baseline.
Other cardiovascular abnormalities seen in our study include bundle branch block (4%) and atrial enlargement (4%).

phenotypes.hpo_label: Ventricular preexcitation with multiple accessory pathways

findings.statement: Forsha et al. (2011) noted that severe ventricular hypertrophy classically associated with infantile Pompe disease was not observed in late-onset patients, and that ECG-defined left ventricular hypertrophy was not specific for increased left ventricular mass: of 10 patients with LVH on ECG, only 1 had elevated LV mass index on echocardiography. No differences were seen between patients with disease duration under vs at least 15 years; 3 of 5 (60%) patients with symptom onset before age 10 had abnormalities. The authors suggested the abnormalities may be related to Pompe disease or to comorbid conditions.
quotes: those such as severe ventricular hypertrophy classically associated with the infantile form of Pompe disease were not noted
Of note, in the 10 patients (12%) with left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG, only one had elevated left ventricular mass index on echocardiography
Of note, in the patients who developed symptoms before 10 years of age, three (60%) had one or more ECG or echocardiographic abnormalities.

findings.statement: Forsha et al. (2011) found that in a double-blind trial in which late-onset Pompe patients were randomized 2:1 to biweekly 20 mg/kg recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase or placebo for 78 weeks, no significant changes in ECG or echocardiographic parameters were associated with enzyme replacement therapy, and no significant cardiovascular safety concerns were identified. One patient with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome had an episode of supraventricular tachycardia after treatment, which was classified as serious and possibly related to the study medication.
quotes: No significant changes in ECG or echocardiographic parameters were seen in association with enzyme replacement therapy compared with placebo.
There were no significant cardiovascular safety concerns associated with enzyme replacement.
The Data Safety Monitoring Board classified this event as serious and possibly related to the study medication.

relevance_reason: Expert consensus guidelines (ACMG) on diagnostic confirmation and management of presymptomatic individuals with several lysosomal storage diseases, including Pompe disease. The abstract gives no Pompe-specific data on late-onset disease.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2011), an ACMG work group, developed educational guidelines for diagnostic confirmation and management of presymptomatic individuals with lysosomal storage diseases, including glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease). These individuals were identified by newborn screening, by family-based testing after a proband was found, or by carrier testing in at-risk populations. The authors noted that the evidence in the literature was limited, so the recommendations should be considered expert opinion.
quotes: To develop educational guidelines for the diagnostic confirmation and management of individuals identified by newborn screening, family-based testing after proband identification, or carrier testing in at-risk populations
Guidelines were developed for Fabry, Gaucher, and Niemann-Pick A/B diseases, glycogen storage type II (Pompe disease)
the evidence in the literature is limited and consequently the recommendations must be considered as expert opinion

relevance_reason: Reports that the ACE insertion/deletion polymorphism is associated with the variable phenotype in a cohort of 38 patients with late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: de Filippi et al. (2010) studied the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) insertion/deletion polymorphism in 38 patients with late-onset Pompe disease, mean age 44.6 years. The genotype frequencies were similar to those of the general population: 16% II, 37% DD, and the rest ID. The 3 genotype groups did not differ in mean age, disease duration, Walton score, or other severity scores. However, the DD genotype was associated with earlier disease onset (P = 0.041), higher creatine kinase levels at diagnosis (P = 0.024), muscle pain (P = 0.014), and faster disease progression (P = 0.037). The authors suggested that the ACE polymorphism may modify the phenotype and prognosis of Pompe disease.
quotes: We included 38 patients with late-onset Pompe disease, aged 44.6 +/- 19.8 years.

The distribution of angiotensin-converting enzyme polymorphism was in line with the general population, with 16% of patients carrying the II genotype, 37% carrying the DD genotype, and the remaining patients with the ID genotype.

The DD polymorphism was associated with earlier onset of disease (P = 0.041), higher creatine kinase levels at diagnosis (P = 0.024), presence of muscle pain (P = 0.014), and more severe rate of disease progression (P = 0.037, analysis of variance test for interaction).

relevance_reason: Review of the diagnosis of glycogenosis type II, including juvenile and adult (late-onset) forms; gives diagnostic criteria based on residual GAA activity.

findings.statement: Bembi et al. (2008) described glycogenosis type II as a progressive, debilitating, and often fatal neuromuscular disorder that occurs as a continuum of clinical phenotypes. These phenotypes vary in organ involvement, age at onset, and severity.
quotes: It is a progressive, debilitating, and often fatal neuromuscular disorder that manifests as a continuum of clinical phenotypes, which vary with respect to organ involvement, age at onset, and severity.

findings.statement: In a review, Bembi et al. (2008) stated that a clinical diagnosis of glycogenosis type II is confirmed by measuring GAA enzyme activity in blood samples, cultured fibroblasts, and muscle biopsies. Activity is virtually absent in infants and markedly reduced in juveniles and adults. The authors also reviewed the use of muscle imaging to evaluate muscle pathology.
quotes: The clinical diagnosis of glycogenosis type II is confirmed by virtual absence (found in infants) and marked reduced activity (found in juveniles and adults) of GAA enzyme in blood samples, cultured fibroblasts, and muscle biopsies.
use of muscle imaging to evaluate muscle pathology is reviewed

relevance_reason: Review of multidisciplinary management and treatment of glycogenosis type II (Pompe disease). It gives management context but no patient data, variants or late-onset-specific results.

findings.statement: Bembi et al. (2008) reviewed the management of glycogenosis type II. They described it as a multisystem disorder that requires care from a multidisciplinary team, including metabolic, cardiology, pulmonology, neurology, neuromuscular, respiratory, physical and occupational therapy, otolaryngology, speech, audiology, genetic counseling and dietetic specialists. They also discussed functional assessment, rehabilitation, nutritional management, genetic counseling, prenatal diagnosis, screening, and emerging therapeutic options.
quotes: Glycogenosis type II is a multisystem disorder that requires management by a multidisciplinary team.
Aspects of functional assessment, rehabilitation, nutritional management, care coordination, nursing, genetic counseling, prenatal diagnosis, and screening are discussed in this article.
In addition, treatment of glycogenosis type II is reviewed with attention to emerging therapeutic options.

relevance_reason: Diagnostic method paper showing that a dried blood spot GAA assay with acarbose inhibition detects late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Kallwass et al. (2007) showed that a fluorometric assay of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) activity in dried blood spots efficiently detected patients with late-onset Pompe disease. The assay used acarbose, a highly selective alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, to remove interference from isoenzymes. The authors noted that late-onset patients are often misdiagnosed by conventional methods because other tissue types retain some GAA activity.
quotes: We recently introduced a simple and reliable method to measure GAA activity in dried blood spots using Acarbose, a highly selective alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, to eliminate isoenzyme interference.
Here we demonstrate that this method efficiently detects late-onset Pompe patients who are frequently misdiagnosed by conventional methods due to residual GAA activity in other tissue types.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It reports ptosis as a feature of late-onset glycogenosis type II, which adds to the clinical phenotype of late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Groen et al. (2006) reported ptosis as a feature of late-onset glycogenosis type II (Pompe disease).
quotes: Ptosis as a feature of late-onset glycogenosis type II.

relevance_reason: Mutation analysis of GAA in 40 Italian patients with late-onset GSDII, including frequent c.-32-13T>G allele and novel variants.

findings.statement: Montalvo et al. (2006) performed complete molecular analysis of the GAA gene in 40 Italian patients with late-onset glycogen storage disease type II and identified 12 novel alleles. Missense mutations were functionally characterized by enzyme activity and protein processing in a human GAA-deficient cell line, and splicing mutations were studied by RT-PCR and in silico analysis. A complex allele carrying three different alterations in cis was also identified.
quotes: We report here the complete molecular analysis of the GAA gene performed on 40 Italian patients with late onset GSDII. Twelve novel alleles have been identified
missense mutations were functionally characterized by enzyme activity and protein processing in a human GAA-deficient cell line while splicing mutations were studied by RT-PCR and in silico analysis
A complex allele was also identified carrying three different alterations in cis.

findings.statement: Montalvo et al. (2006) found that the c.-32-13T-G GAA mutation was the most frequent mutation among 40 Italian patients with late-onset GSDII, present in compound heterozygous state in 85% of patients (allele frequency 42.3%), as described in other late-onset Caucasian populations.
quotes: The c.-32-13T > G was the most frequent mutation, present as compound heterozygote in 85% of the patients (allele frequency 42.3%), as described in other late onset GSDII Caucasian populations.

findings.statement: Montalvo et al. (2006) found the c.-32-13T-G mutation in association with the c.2237G-A (W746X) nonsense mutation in 9 of 40 Italian patients with late-onset GSDII, and discussed genotype-phenotype correlations with emphasis on this subgroup.
quotes: Interestingly, the c.-32-13T > G was associated with the c.2237G > A (p.W746X) in nine of the 40 patients.
Genotype-phenotype correlations are discussed with particular emphasis on the subgroup carrying the c.-32-13T > G/c.2237G > A genotype.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It reports a family with two clinical forms of glycogen storage disease type II across two generations, which is relevant to the variable onset of late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Amartino et al. (2006) reported two clinical forms of glycogen storage disease type II in two generations of the same family.
quotes: Two clinical forms of glycogen-storage disease type II in two generations of the same family.

relevance_reason: Questionnaire-based study of 255 children and adults with Pompe disease, mostly late-onset, relating disease severity to disease duration and age at onset.

findings.statement: Hagemans et al. (2005) used a questionnaire to collect information on 255 children and adults with Pompe disease. Disease severity was associated with how long patients had had the disease, not with their age. Earlier disease manifestation meant that patients became dependent on a wheelchair or ventilator earlier.
quotes: Information about 255 children and adults with Pompe disease was gathered through a questionnaire.
Disease severity was associated with disease duration and not with age; an early manifestation of the disease implied earlier wheelchair or ventilator dependency.

findings.statement: Hagemans et al. (2005) found that patients under 15 years of age included a subgroup whose disease was more severe and progressed more rapidly. The authors suggested that these patients need more intensive follow-up and early intervention, before irreversible damage occurs.
quotes: The patient group under age 15 included a subgroup with a more severe and rapid course of the disease.
They require more intensive follow-up and early intervention, before irreversible damage has occurred.

relevance_reason: This case report describes a patient with late-onset Pompe disease who had a new vascular finding and two novel GAA mutations.

findings.statement: Anneser et al. (2005) described a 30-year-old woman with late-onset Pompe disease. She had vascular involvement that resembled the atherosclerotic angiopathy of the elderly, which the authors considered an unusual phenotype.
quotes: The authors describe a 30-year-old woman affected by late-onset Pompe disease with vascular affection resembling atherosclerotic angiopathy of the elderly.

relevance_reason: Reports a Chinese family with juvenile-onset GSDII and novel compound heterozygous GAA mutations, with intrafamilial phenotypic variation.

findings.statement: Lam et al. (2003) described a 16-year-old Chinese patient with juvenile-onset glycogen storage disease type II (GSDII). His 13-year-old brother was asymptomatic despite carrying the same genotype. The authors concluded that intrafamilial phenotypic variation of juvenile-onset GSDII is ethnically diverse and suggested that other genes contribute to the phenotypic variability of GSDII.
quotes: define the juvenile-onset glycogen storage disease type II (GSDII) in a 16-year-old Chinese patient
The asymptomatic 13-year-old brother of the proband is also a compound heterozygote of the two mutations.
These results confirm that intrafamilial phenotypic variation of juvenile-onset GSDII is ethnically diverse and suggest the contribution of other genes to the phenotypic variability of GSDII.

phenotypes.text: juvenile-onset glycogen storage disease type II

findings.statement: In a 16-year-old Chinese patient with juvenile-onset GSDII, Lam et al. (2003) identified compound heterozygosity for 2 novel mutations in the acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) gene, P361L and R437C. His asymptomatic 13-year-old brother was also a compound heterozygote for the 2 mutations.
quotes: The authors describe two novel mutations of the acid alpha-glucosidase gene, P361L and R437C, which define the juvenile-onset glycogen storage disease type II (GSDII) in a 16-year-old Chinese patient.
The asymptomatic 13-year-old brother of the proband is also a compound heterozygote of the two mutations.

relevance_reason: Clinical, biochemical and genetic study of 21 French patients with juvenile/adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, including GAA mutations and genotype-phenotype analysis.

findings.statement: Laforêt et al. (2000) studied 21 unrelated French patients with juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. Progressive muscle weakness began in adulthood in all but 1 patient, but 16 patients had mild, nonprogressive muscular symptoms that started in childhood. Eighteen patients had a similar pattern of pelvic girdle weakness, mostly affecting the glutei and thigh adductors. Eight patients had restrictive respiratory insufficiency with vital capacity below 60%, and in 2 patients respiratory failure was the first sign of disease.
quotes: The authors performed a clinical, biochemical, and genetic study on 21 unrelated patients with juvenile and adult-onset AMD.

Although onset of progressive muscle weakness occurred during adulthood in all cases but one, presence of mild, nonprogressive muscular symptoms appearing during childhood was detected in 16 patients.
Restrictive respiratory insufficiency with vital capacity less than 60% was noted in eight patients, and respiratory failure was the first manifestation in two cases.

phenotypes.text: mild nonprogressive muscular symptoms in childhood
pelvic girdle muscle weakness predominating in glutei and thigh adductors
restrictive respiratory insufficiency with vital capacity <60%

findings.statement: Of the 21 French patients with juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency studied by Laforêt et al. (2000), 17 carried the IVS1-13T-G transversion in the GAA gene. One of these patients was homozygous for it; the others carried it as one allele. All patients except 1 were compound heterozygotes.
quotes: All patients but one were compound heterozygotes, and 17 carried the IVS1 (-13T ---> G) transversion (one patient was homozygous for this mutation).

findings.statement: Laforêt et al. (2000) found both mutant GAA alleles in 10 of the 21 patients and detected 13 different mutations in total. They concluded that juvenile and adult acid maltase deficiency is genetically highly heterogeneous in the French population.
quotes: The two mutated alleles were identified in 10 cases, with 13 different mutations detected in the GAA gene.
This study shows a high genetic heterogeneity of juvenile and adult AMD in the French population.

findings.statement: Laforêt et al. (2000) found no clear correlation between type of GAA mutation and phenotype in juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. They suggested this pointed to a complex disease mechanism that needs further study.
quotes: There was no clear correlation between the type of mutation and phenotype.
The absence of genotype-phenotype correlation suggests a complex physiopathology that requires further investigations.

relevance_reason: Clinical, biochemical and genetic study of 18 adult-onset GSD II patients evaluating diagnostic tests and proposing a diagnostic protocol.

findings.statement: Ausems et al. (1999) performed a clinical, biochemical, and genetic study of 18 patients with adult-onset GSD II to assess the diagnostic value of laboratory tests. Measurement of GAA activity in muscle and histopathologic analysis of muscle tissue appeared to have no additional value when GAA activity in leukocytes was clearly deficient, and creatine kinase elevation was a sensitive marker of the disease. The authors formulated a diagnostic protocol.
quotes: we performed a clinical, biochemical, and genetic study of 18 patients with this disease

Measurement of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) activity in muscle and histopathologic analysis of muscle tissue appeared to have no additional value when GAA activity in leukocytes was clearly deficient.
Our study showed that creatine kinase elevation is a sensitive marker of GSD II. A diagnostic protocol is formulated.

phenotypes.text: deficient acid alpha-glucosidase activity in leukocytes
phenotypes.hpo_label: Abnormal leukocyte enzyme concentration or activity

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It indicates a population study of carrier frequency for glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) in New York and estimates of how many affected individuals are born with it, which is relevant to population genetics.

findings.statement: Martiniuk et al. (1998) determined the carrier frequency for glycogen storage disease type II in New York and estimated how many affected individuals are born with the disease.
quotes: Carrier frequency for glycogen storage disease type II in New York and estimates of affected individuals born with the disease.

relevance_reason: Reports a Gaa knockout mouse model that reproduces features of the infantile and adult forms of GSD II, including diaphragm involvement and late muscle wasting. It belongs in the animal model section.

findings.statement: Raben et al. (1998) used gene targeting to disrupt the acid alpha-glucosidase gene in mice. Homozygous 6(neo)/6(neo) mice had no enzyme activity. Glycogen began to build up in cardiac and skeletal muscle lysosomes by 3 weeks of age and increased progressively, and by 3.5 weeks the mice had markedly reduced mobility and strength. The mice grew normally, reached adulthood and remained fertile. As in the human adult disease, older mice accumulated glycogen in the diaphragm, and by 8 to 9 months they developed obvious muscle wasting and a weak, waddling gait. The authors concluded that the model recapitulates critical features of both the infantile and adult forms of the disease.
quotes: mice homozygous for disruption of the acid alpha-glucosidase gene (6(neo)/6(neo)) lack enzyme activity and begin to accumulate glycogen in cardiac and skeletal muscle lysosomes by 3 weeks of age, with a progressive increase thereafter

They grow normally, however, reach adulthood, remain fertile, and, as in the human adult disease, older mice accumulate glycogen in the diaphragm. By 8-9 months of age animals develop obvious muscle wasting and a weak, waddling gait.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Glycogen accumulation in muscle fiber lysosomes

findings.statement: Raben et al. (1998) also made a second Gaa mouse model with deletion of exon 6 (Delta6/Delta6). Like the exon 13 knockout, these mice kept normal strength and mobility up to 6.5 months of age, even though their biochemical and pathological changes could not be distinguished from those of the 6(neo)/6(neo) mice. The authors suggested that the genetic background of the mouse strains contributes to the differences among the three models.
quotes: in a second model, mutant mice with deletion of exon 6 (Delta6/Delta6)
have unimpaired strength and mobility (up to 6.5 months of age) despite indistinguishable biochemical and pathological changes
The genetic background of the mouse strains appears to contribute to the differences among the three models.

relevance_reason: The paper describes a Gaa knockout mouse model of GSDII/Pompe disease. Its slowly progressive course, with no overt symptoms at 9 months, is relevant as an animal model for the Pompe disease entries.

findings.statement: Bijvoet et al. (1998) generated a mouse model of GSDII (Pompe disease) by targeted disruption of the murine acid alpha-glucosidase gene (Gaa) in embryonic stem cells. Homozygous knockout (Gaa -/-) mice lacked Gaa mRNA and had a virtually complete acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Glycogen-containing lysosomes were detected soon after birth in liver, heart, and skeletal muscle cells. By 13 weeks of age, large focal glycogen deposits had formed, and vacuolar spaces stained positive for acid phosphatase, indicating lysosomal pathology.
quotes: A mouse model of this disease was obtained by targeted disruption of the murine acid alpha-glucosidase gene (Gaa) in embryonic stem cells. Homozygous knockout mice (Gaa -/-) lack Gaa mRNA and have a virtually complete acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
Glycogen-containing lysosomes are detected soon after birth in liver, heart and skeletal muscle cells. By 13 weeks of age, large focal deposits of glycogen have formed.
Vacuolar spaces stain positive for acid phosphatase as a sign of lysosomal pathology.

phenotypes.text: lysosomal glycogen storage in liver, heart and skeletal muscle

findings.statement: Bijvoet et al. (1998) found that male and female Gaa knockout mice were fertile. At 9 months of age, the oldest knockout mice still had no overt clinical symptoms, but their hearts were typically enlarged and their electrocardiograms were abnormal.
quotes: Both male and female knockout mice are fertile and can be intercrossed to produce progeny.
Overt clinical symptoms are still absent, but the heart is typically enlarged and the electrocardiogram is abnormal.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It describes a study of how often three common GAA mutant alleles occur, and which clinical phenotypes go with them, in 121 patients with glycogen storage disease type II. That is relevant to late-onset Pompe disease, but the title gives no detail on the alleles or the phenotypes.

findings.statement: Kroos et al. (1995) studied how often three common mutant alleles occurred in 121 patients with glycogen storage disease type II and which clinical phenotypes were associated with them.
quotes: Glycogen storage disease type II: frequency of three common mutant alleles and their associated clinical phenotypes studied in 121 patients.

relevance_reason: A clinical, biochemical and genetic study of 16 patients with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, reporting their GAA genotypes and how genotype relates to phenotype.

findings.statement: Wokke et al. (1995) studied 16 patients from 11 families with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency and found that all were compound heterozygotes who carried the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion on one allele.
quotes: We performed a clinical, biochemical, and genetic study in 16 patients from 11 families with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. All patients were compound heterozygotes and carried the IVS1(-13T --> G) transversion on one allele

findings.statement: In 7 of the 11 probands (64%) with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, Wokke et al. (1995) found a deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2 of the GAA gene on the second allele, in trans with the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion.
quotes: the second allele harbored either a deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2 (7 probands, 64%) or a deletion of exon 18 (1 proband, 9%)

variants.as_reported: deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2

findings.statement: In 1 of the 11 probands (9%), Wokke et al. (1995) found a deletion of exon 18 of the GAA gene on the second allele, in trans with the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion.
quotes: the second allele harbored either a deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2 (7 probands, 64%) or a deletion of exon 18 (1 proband, 9%)

findings.statement: In the 16 patients with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency studied by Wokke et al. (1995), worsening of handicap was related to age, and the decline in vital capacity was related to how long the patient had had symptoms. Respiratory insufficiency was never the first manifestation. Muscle weakness progressed over a period of years.
quotes: Deterioration of handicap was related to age, and decrease in vital capacity to duration of the symptomatic stage. Respiratory insufficiency was never the first manifestation.
progression of muscle weakness over a period of years

findings.statement: Wokke et al. (1995) found that serum creatine kinase activity and alpha-glucosidase activity in peripheral blood cells or muscle were helpful for diagnosis but did not have prognostic value.
quotes: The levels of activity of serum creatine kinase and of alpha-glucosidase in peripheral blood cells or muscle were helpful for the diagnosis, but did not have prognostic value.

findings.statement: Wokke et al. (1995) concluded that the adult form of acid maltase deficiency appears to be fairly homogeneous both clinically and genetically. They suggested that reduced alpha-glucosidase activity is the final common pathway that leads to destruction of muscle fibers and progressive muscle weakness.
quotes: The adult form of acid maltase deficiency appears to be both clinically and genetically rather homogeneous; decrease of alpha-glucosidase activity is the final common pathway leading to destruction of muscle fibers and progression of muscle weakness over a period of years.

relevance_reason: The title links cardiac arrhythmias with the adult (late-onset) form of type II glycogenosis. Only the title was available, so no details could be extracted.

findings.statement: Francesconi and Auff (1982) reported cardiac arrhythmias in association with the adult form of type II glycogenosis (glycogen storage disease II).
quotes: Cardiac arrhythmias and the adult form of type II glycogenosis.

relevance_reason: Case report of adult-onset acid maltase deficiency that presented as diaphragmatic paralysis, with the diagnosis confirmed biochemically.

findings.statement: Sivak et al. (1981) reported a 51-year-old man with a 6-year history of gradually progressive exertional dyspnea. At first this was attributed to increasing age, but evaluation eventually showed diaphragmatic paralysis. Neurologic examination found only minimal weakness of the limb muscles. Exercise stress testing was needed to define the limits of his exercise tolerance.
quotes: A 51-year-old man presented with a six-year history of gradually progressive exertional dyspnea.
His complaint was attributed to increasing age, but evaluation finally led to a diagnosis of diaphragmatic paralysis.
Neurological examination disclosed only minimal evidence of weakness of limb muscles.

findings.statement: In the patient reported by Sivak et al. (1981), electromyographic studies suggested acid maltase deficiency. Electron microscopic and biochemical studies of a muscle biopsy confirmed the diagnosis.
quotes: Electromyographic studies suggested a diagnosis of acid maltase deficiency, which was confirmed by electron microscopic and biochemical studies of muscle biopsy sections.

relevance_reason: The abstract reports enzyme protein (CRM) studies in fibroblasts from patients with adult-form acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, showing molecular heterogeneity within the late-onset form and between it and the infantile form.

findings.statement: Beratis et al. (1983) studied cultured fibroblasts from 3 patients with the adult form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. In 2 strains, rocket immunoelectrophoresis showed less enzyme protein, and the reduction was directly proportional to the reduction in enzyme activity. The third adult-form strain had activity within the range of the infantile form, and no crossreacting material (CRM) could be identified. The authors concluded that there was molecular heterogeneity within the adult form as well as between the clinical forms.
quotes: In two fibroblast strains with the adult form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, rocket immunoelectrophoresis demonstrated a reduction in the amount of enzyme protein, which was directly proportional to the reduction in enzyme activity.
In another fibroblast strain obtained from a patient with the adult form of the disease, the activity was within the range of the infantile form and no CRM could be identified.
Molecular differences were identified both between the clinical forms of the disease and within the infantile and the adult forms of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.

phenotypes.text: reduced acid alpha-glucosidase activity in fibroblasts

findings.statement: Beratis et al. (1983) found that of 9 fibroblast strains from patients with the infantile form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, 8 were CRM-negative and 1 was CRM-positive by both agar immunodiffusion and immunotitration. Apparent enzyme activity did not differ between the CRM-negative and CRM-positive infantile strains.
quotes: Of nine fibroblast strains derived from patients with the infantile form of the disease, eight were crossreacting material (CRM)-negative and one CRM-positive.
No difference in apparent enzymatic activity was observed between CRM-negative and CRM-positive infantile acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts.

findings.statement: Beratis et al. (1983) found that fibroblasts with phenotype 2 of acid alpha-glucosidase, which is considered a normal variant, had less enzyme protein and a reduced ability to cleave glycogen, but normal catalytic activity toward maltose. The authors stated that it remains unknown whether isozyme 2 homozygotes have enough enzyme deficiency to cause glycogen accumulation and a muscular dystrophy-like disease later in life.
quotes: Fibroblasts with phenotype 2 of acid alpha-glucosidase, considered a normal variant, showed a reduction both in the amount of enzyme protein and in the ability of the enzyme to cleave glycogen. However, the catalytic activity for maltose was normal.

It remains unknown whether or not the enzyme deficiency in homozygotes for isozyme 2 of acid alpha-glucosidase will be sufficient to cause glycogen accumulation and lead to the development of muscular dystrophy-like disease later in life.

relevance_reason: Single-patient report of high-protein diet therapy in a child with acid maltase deficiency (later-onset muscle weakness) with pathogenesis hypothesis; relevant to clinical management.

findings.statement: Slonim et al. (1983) treated a child with acid maltase deficiency and progressive muscle weakness with a high-protein diet for 12 months, which reversed the weakness and wasting, with improvement in muscle function, exercise tolerance, and growth.
quotes: To reduce this muscle catabolism, the patient was treated with a high-protein diet for 12 months. This has reversed the weakness and wasting, with improvement in muscle function, exercise tolerance, and growth.

findings.statement: Slonim et al. (1983) observed a rapid fall in circulating branched chain amino acids after protein ingestion in a child with acid maltase deficiency, suggesting that increased net muscle protein catabolism may play a part in the pathogenesis of the progressive muscle weakness, in addition to intralysosomal glycogen accumulation and altered myofibrillar morphology.
quotes: A rapid fall in circulating branched chain amino acids after protein ingestion in a child with AMD suggested that increased net muscle protein catabolism may play a part in the pathogenesis of this condition.
Progressive muscle weakness in acid maltase deficiency (AMD) is associated with intralysosomal accumulation of glycogen and altered myofibrillar morphology.

phenotypes.text: rapid fall in plasma branched chain amino acids after protein ingestion
phenotypes.hpo_label: Abnormal circulating branched-chain amino acid concentration

relevance_reason: Clinical, biochemical and muscle pathology description of three children with the childhood form of acid maltase deficiency (late-onset Pompe disease).

findings.statement: Matsuishi et al. (1984) studied 3 children with the childhood form of acid maltase deficiency (glycogenosis type II), including 2 sibs and 1 sporadic patient. Features included delayed developmental milestones and mild generalized muscle weakness. The authors considered nasal vocalization and an EMG finding of abnormal insertion voltage followed by pseudomyotonic discharge to be characteristic diagnostic findings for the childhood form.
quotes: Three children, including two siblings and a patient with sporadic glycogenosis type II (childhood form of acid maltase deficiency [AMD] ), were studied clinically, biochemically, and morphologically.

In addition to a delay in developmental milestones and mild generalized muscle weakness, nasal vocalization and an electromyographic finding of abnormal insertion voltage, followed by pseudomyotonic discharge, were assumed to be characteristic diagnostic findings for the childhood form of AMD.

phenotypes.text: abnormal insertion voltage and pseudomyotonic discharges on EMG

findings.statement: Matsuishi et al. (1984) found that neutral maltase activity was highest in the muscle biopsy from the patient with the least severe weakness among 3 children with childhood acid maltase deficiency, and suggested that this enzyme may play a role in reducing muscle involvement.
quotes: Since the neutral maltase activity was highest in the muscle biopsy specimen from the patient with the least severe weakness, the enzyme may play a role in reducing muscle involvement.

findings.statement: Matsuishi et al. (1984) found selective type 2A fiber atrophy and type 2B fiber deficiency in affected muscles as common histochemical findings in the childhood form of acid maltase deficiency.
quotes: Selective type 2A fiber atrophy and type 2B fiber deficiency in the affected muscles were the common histochemical findings in this particular form of AMD.

relevance_reason: The title describes adult-onset myopathy caused by glycogen storage disease from acid maltase deficiency, which is the subject of this entry (late-onset Pompe disease). Only the title was available.

findings.statement: Hudgson et al. (1968) described adult myopathy caused by glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency.
quotes: Adult myopathy from glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It says the paper is about late infantile acid maltase deficiency, which is a later-onset form of Pompe disease and therefore the subject of this entry. No other details are available.

findings.statement: Swaiman et al. (1968) reported on late infantile acid maltase deficiency.
quotes: Late infantile acid maltase deficiency.

relevance_reason: The title describes studies of four adult patients with acid maltase deficiency, which is the subject of this entry (late-onset Pompe disease). Only the title was available.

findings.statement: Engel (1970) reported studies in 4 adults with acid maltase deficiency. In these patients the syndrome could mimic muscular dystrophy or other myopathies.
quotes: Acid maltase deficiency in adults: studies in four cases of a syndrome which may mimic muscular dystrophy or other myopathies.

relevance_reason: Only the title was available. It reports abnormalities in fibroblasts cultured from patients with adult acid maltase deficiency, which is relevant to late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Angelini et al. (1972) reported abnormalities in fibroblasts cultured from patients with adult acid maltase deficiency.
quotes: Adult acid maltase deficiency. Abnormalities in fibroblasts cultured from patients.

relevance_reason: Case series of 5 adults with late-onset acid maltase deficiency describing clinical features, diagnosis, and long-term ventilatory management.

findings.statement: Trend et al. (1985) described 5 patients with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency whose initial pelvic girdle symptoms began late in the second or early in the third decade, followed some years later by signs of respiratory insufficiency. Typically the patients were tall, with weak and wasted paraspinal and gluteal muscles and lower limb weakness; all were orthopneic with marked diaphragmatic weakness.
quotes: All patients had developed their initial pelvic girdle symptoms late in the second or early in the third decade and some years later developed signs of respiratory insufficiency.
Typically they were tall, had weak and wasted paraspinal and gluteal muscles with lower limb weakness. All were orthopnoeic with marked diaphragmatic weakness.

phenotypes.onset: late second or early third decade

findings.statement: Trend et al. (1985) found characteristic glycogen vacuoles in peripheral blood lymphocytes in all 5 patients, whereas muscle biopsy was characteristic in only 1 of 4 cases and showed minimal or nonspecific features in 3. Diagnosis was confirmed by acid maltase enzyme assay in muscle and cultured fibroblasts.
quotes: In all patients characteristic glycogen vacuoles were seen in peripheral blood lymphocytes.
Muscle biopsy was characteristic in only 1 out of 4 cases and showed minimal or nonspecific features in 3.
The diagnosis was confirmed by enzyme assay in muscle and cultured fibroblasts.

phenotypes.text: glycogen vacuoles in peripheral blood lymphocytes
characteristic vacuolar myopathy on muscle biopsy

findings.statement: Trend et al. (1985) reported that long-term domiciliary ventilatory support (25 patient-years) using a rocking bed or intermittent positive pressure respiration via tracheostomy allowed all 5 patients to return to work, with clinical condition remaining stable.
quotes: Long-term domiciliary ventilatory support (25 patient-years) using a rocking bed or intermittent positive pressure respiration with a tracheostomy has allowed a return to work in all patients, with their clinical condition remaining stable.

relevance_reason: The abstract describes adult-onset familial bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis in twin brothers but does not mention acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency or Pompe disease. The authors report that no metabolic disorder of the neuromuscular system was detected. The paper is relevant only as context: diaphragmatic paralysis is a recognized presentation of late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Molho et al. (1987) described 2 homozygote (identical) twin brothers who both developed bilateral paralysis of the diaphragm at age 50. Over 4 years of follow-up, no infectious, metabolic, degenerative, or proliferative disorder of the neuromuscular system and no thoracic disease that could explain the lesion was found. The authors concluded that it appeared to be an isolated lesion of genetic origin.
quotes: At age 50 two homozygote twin brothers developed bilateral paralysis of the diaphragm.
No infectious, metabolic, degenerative or proliferative disorders of the neuromuscular system and no thoracic diseases which could explain this lesion were detected during four years of follow-up.
It appears thus to be an isolated lesion of genetic origin.

relevance_reason: Reports a sibship with late-onset alpha-glucosidase deficiency (proximal myopathy) and basilar artery aneurysms associated with vascular smooth muscle glycogen deposition.

findings.statement: Makos et al. (1987) reported 3 brothers, sons of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, who developed progressive proximal muscle weakness due to alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Each developed a fusiform basilar artery aneurysm; the aneurysm ruptured fatally in 2 of the brothers and was complicated by cerebellar infarction in the third.
quotes: Three sons of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents developed progressive proximal muscular weakness secondary to alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
Each patient developed a fusiform basilar artery aneurysm, which was complicated by fatal rupture in two patients and a cerebellar infarction in the third.

findings.statement: In the brothers reported by Makos et al. (1987), postmortem examination showed severe vacuolation of skeletal muscle, liver, and vascular smooth muscle with accumulation of PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive material; in the surviving brother, similar glycogen deposition was shown in smooth muscle of the superficial temporal artery. The authors suggested that basilar artery aneurysm formation may be a consequence of alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
quotes: Postmortem examination demonstrated severe vacuolation of skeletal muscle, liver, and vascular smooth muscle with accumulation of periodic acid-Schiff-positive, diastase-sensitive material.
In the surviving brother, similar glycogen deposition was demonstrated in the smooth muscle of the superficial temporal artery.
Basilar artery aneurysm formation in this sibship may be a consequence of alpha-glucosidase deficiency.

phenotypes.text: skeletal muscle vacuolation with glycogen accumulation
glycogen deposition in vascular smooth muscle

relevance_reason: An abstract-only series of 18 Israeli patients with GAA deficiency. Almost all had the infantile form, and only one had the juvenile (late-onset) type. It gives context on enzyme heterogeneity and on Arab prevalence.

findings.statement: Bashan et al. (1988) reported 18 patients with alpha-glucosidase deficiency diagnosed in Israel over 15 years. All were Palestinian Arabs except 2 sibs from a Jewish Iraqi family. All had the infantile type (Pompe disease) except 1 patient, who had the juvenile type.
quotes: Eighteen patients with alpha-glucosidase deficiency have been diagnosed in Israel during the last 15 years. All patients were Palestinian Arabs, with the exception of two siblings from a Jewish Iraqi family.
Clinically all patients had the infantile type (Pompe's disease), except one who had the juvenile type.

findings.statement: Among the patients reported by Bashan et al. (1988), muscle glycogen content ranged from 4 to 17% of wet weight. Muscle alpha-glucosidase activity was zero in 10 of 17 patients tested, and in the 7 with residual activity the highest value was 18% of normal. Leukocyte alpha-glucosidase activity was highly variable, so the authors judged leukocytes unsuitable for enzymatic diagnosis. pH profiles of muscle and leukocyte enzyme activity showed marked heterogeneity.
quotes: Muscle glycogen content varied from 4 to 17% wet weight. Muscle alpha-glucosidase activity was zero in 10 of 17 patients examined.
Among the seven patients in whom residual activity was present, the highest value was 18% of normal.
Leukocyte alpha-glucosidase activity was highly variable, making this tissue unfit for enzymatic diagnosis of the disease.

findings.statement: Bashan et al. (1988) noted a high prevalence of alpha-glucosidase deficiency in the Arab population of Israel, a population with a high rate of consanguinity.
quotes: A high prevalence of the disease in the Arab population was noted.
In spite of a high rate of consanguinity, only a small number of autosomal recessively inherited diseases have been shown to be unusually prevalent in the Arab population.

relevance_reason: Case report of an adult patient with acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency who responded well to a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet. It is relevant to the clinical management of late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Isaacs et al. (1986) fully investigated an adult patient with lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. The patient was then given several forms of therapy and responded favorably to a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet.
quotes: An adult patient with lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency was fully investigated, and then placed on various forms of therapy with favourable response to a high protein, low carbohydrate diet.

findings.statement: Isaacs et al. (1986) discussed how acid maltase deficiency relates to muscle weakness and to glycogenosome formation, with or without accumulation of glycogen inside the muscle fibers.
quotes: the problem of acid maltase deficiency and the relationship to weakness and glycogenosome formation with accumulation or otherwise of glycogen within the muscle fibres is discussed.

relevance_reason: Case report of adult-onset acid maltase deficiency with respiratory muscle weakness treated with high-protein diet; relevant to clinical features and management of late-onset Pompe disease.

findings.statement: Margolis and Hill (1986) described a 55-year-old man with adult acid maltase deficiency (AMD) and severe ventilatory muscle weakness. The authors noted that AMD in the adult is associated with progressive ventilatory muscle weakness and death from respiratory failure.
quotes: Acid maltase deficiency (AMD) in the adult is associated with progressive ventilatory muscle weakness and death from respiratory failure
we treated a 55-yr-old man with AMD and severe ventilatory muscle weakness

phenotypes.hpo_label: Respiratory insufficiency due to muscle weakness

findings.statement: Margolis and Hill (1986) treated a 55-year-old man with adult AMD and severe ventilatory muscle weakness with a high-protein (1.6 g/kg), weight-reducing diet for 27 months, based on evidence that muscle catabolism may contribute to weakness. The therapy was associated with striking improvement in respiratory function, including measures of ventilatory muscle strength and endurance, and the authors suggested that high-protein dietary therapy may be useful in adults with AMD and respiratory insufficiency.
quotes: we treated a 55-yr-old man with AMD and severe ventilatory muscle weakness with a high-protein (1.6 g/kg), weight-reducing diet for 27 months
High-protein dietary therapy was associated with striking improvement in respiratory function, including measures of ventilatory muscle strength and endurance.
We suggest that high-protein dietary therapy may be useful in adults with AMD and respiratory insufficiency.

relevance_reason: Describes a dominantly inherited cardioskeletal myopathy with lysosomal glycogen storage but normal acid maltase activity. It is a phenocopy of acid maltase deficiency, so it is relevant to differential diagnosis and heterogeneity, not to GAA-deficient late-onset Pompe disease itself.

findings.statement: Byrne et al. (1986) described a family in which 7 members over 3 generations had a cardioskeletal myopathy. Muscle biopsy showed a vacuolar myopathy with excess free and intralysosomal glycogen storage, but acid maltase activity was normal. The authors called this the third report of lysosomal glycogen storage disease without acid maltase deficiency. They noted that, unusually among the glycogenoses, it had a dominant inheritance pattern.
quotes: A family is presented in which 7 members over 3 generations were affected by cardioskeletal myopathy.
This is the third report of non-acid maltase deficient lysosomal glycogen storage disease
This syndrome is unusual among glycogenoses in having a dominant inheritance pattern.

findings.statement: In the family reported by Byrne et al. (1986), biopsies showed a vacuolar myopathy with excessive free and intralysosomal glycogen storage in both skeletal and cardiac striated muscle. Postmortem studies in several patients showed changes of congestive cardiomyopathy with myocardial fibrosis.
quotes: A vacuolar myopathy with excessive free and intralysosomal glycogen storage in skeletal and cardiac striated muscle was identified in biopsy studies.
Post-mortem studies in several patients revealed changes of a congestive cardiomyopathy with myocardial fibrosis.

findings.statement: Byrne et al. (1986) found normal levels of acid maltase, phosphorylase and debrancher enzyme in skeletal muscle from 1 affected family member. Lysosomal enzyme screens and glycolytic enzyme levels were also normal.
quotes: Acid maltase, phosphorylase, debrancher and lysosomal enzyme screens, and glycolytic enzyme levels in skeletal muscle, were normal in 1 case.

relevance_reason: Case report of late-onset acid maltase deficiency with cerebral arterial vacuolar degeneration and intracerebral aneurysms, describing vascular and CNS involvement.

findings.statement: Kretzschmar et al. (1990) reported a patient with late-onset acid maltase deficiency who had marked liver and skeletal muscle involvement. Unlike other adult cases, the patient had CNS pathology: white matter areas that were hypodense on CT and hyperintense on MRI, and myelin changes ranging from focal demyelination to necrosis.
quotes: We present a case of late-onset acid maltase deficiency (AMD) with pronounced involvement of the liver and skeletal muscles.
the case presented here shows CNS pathology with hypodense and hyperintense white matter areas on CT and MRI scans, and myelin changes ranging from focal areas of demyelination to necrosis.

phenotypes.text: white matter abnormalities on CT and MRI

findings.statement: In their patient with late-onset acid maltase deficiency, Kretzschmar et al. (1990) found vacuolar degeneration of small and large cerebral arteries. Vacuoles in pericytes and arterial smooth muscle cells were partly filled with PAS-positive material. Electron microscopy showed lysosomal and free cytoplasmic glycogen in intimal smooth muscle cells of large cerebral arteries and in pericytes of arterioles and capillaries. Local glycogen accumulation was associated with severe cell damage and necrosis. The authors thought that this damage to the vessel walls caused the many small intracerebral aneurysms and suggested that the vascular pathology underlay the neuropathologic changes.
quotes: Neuropathologic changes seem to be related to unusual vascular pathology consisting of vacuolar degeneration of small and large arterial blood vessels.
Electron microscopy revealed lysosomal and cytoplasmic free glycogen in smooth muscle cells in the intima of large cerebral arteries as well as in pericytes of arterioles and capillaries.
The formation of a great number of small aneurysms of intracerebral arteries is thought to be the result of cell damage in the vessel walls.

relevance_reason: Case report of late-onset acid maltase deficiency (myopathy) in a 68-year-old man; only the title was available.

findings.statement: Chancellor et al. (1991) reported a 68-year-old man with acid maltase deficiency who presented with a myopathy and urinary incontinence brought on by exercise.
quotes: Acid maltase deficiency presenting with a myopathy and exercise induced urinary incontinence in a 68 year old male.

relevance_reason: The abstract describes alveolar hypoventilation caused by bilateral diaphragm paralysis or weakness in 8 patients, 7 of whom had a generalized neuromuscular disorder. It does not name acid maltase deficiency, Pompe disease or GAA, so from this text it only gives context on diaphragm involvement in neuromuscular disease.

findings.statement: Davis et al. (1976) studied 8 patients with diaphragm weakness, suggested by inward movement of the abdominal wall on breathing in. Seven of the 8 had evidence of a generalized neuromuscular disorder. The change in pressure across the diaphragm during a maximum breath in was zero in 5 patients and 2 to 6 cm H2O in the other 3 (normal more than 25 cm H2O), indicating paralysis or severe weakness. Vital capacity was 30 to 65% of predicted when upright and typically fell by about half when lying down.
quotes: Eight patients were studied in whom diaphragm weakness had been suggested by paradoxical (inward) movement of the abdominal wall on inspiration, of whom seven had evidence of a generalized neuromuscular disorder.
In five patients, deltaPDi was zero and in the others ranged from 2-6 cm H2O (normal greater than 25 cm H2O) indicating paralysis and severe weakness in the respective groups.
Vital capacity ranged from 65-30 per cent of the predicted normal in the upright posture, typically falling by about a half in the supine posture.

phenotypes.text: paradoxical inward abdominal wall movement on inspiration
bilateral diaphragm paralysis or severe weakness

findings.statement: Davis et al. (1976) found alveolar hypoventilation in 5 patients when lying down and in 6 when asleep. Sleep worsened blood gases much more in these patients than in normal subjects. The patients breathed faster than age-matched controls and had an impaired ventilatory response to CO2. The hypoventilation was associated with disturbed sleep, morning headache and daytime fatigue.
quotes: Alveolar hypoventilation was present in five patients when supine and in six when asleep, the deterioration in blood gases associated with sleep generally being much greater in these patients than in normal subjects.
Respiratory rate was significantly greater than age-matched controls. The ventilatory response to CO2 was impaired.
Alveolar hypoventilation was associated with disturbed sleep, morning headache and day-time fatigue.

findings.statement: Davis et al. (1976) found that fluoroscopy of the diaphragm gave misleading results in assessing diaphragm function. Patients could bring PCO2 to normal by deliberately breathing faster and deeper, so the authors stressed that voluntary breathing tests of this kind are unreliable measures of ventilatory reserve.
quotes: Fluoroscopy of the diaphragm was found to give misleading results, and the resons for this are considered.
The PCO2 could be brought to normal levels by voluntary hyperventilation, and the unreliability of voluntary respiratory manoeuvres of this kind as indices of ventilatory reserve is emphasized.

findings.statement: Davis et al. (1976) reported that patients with alveolar hypoventilation due to diaphragm paralysis improved in their symptoms when they used a cuirass respirator at night.
quotes: Symptomatic benefit was achieved by the use of a cuirass respirator at night.

relevance_reason: Describes a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, with the muscle pathology and enzyme deficiency reproduced in cultured muscle.

findings.statement: Askanas et al. (1976) established muscle tissue cultures from the biopsy of a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. Acid maltase (pH 4.0) activity, measured by maltose hydrolysis, was undetectable in both the cultured and the biopsied muscle. Acid phosphatase, another lysosomal enzyme, was increased in both.
quotes: We established muscle-tissue cultures from biopsy of a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency.

Acid maltase (pH 4.0), a lysosomal enzyme, was undetectable in either cultured or biopsied muscle by maltose hydrolysis, whereas acid phosphatase, also a lysosomal enzyme, was increased in both sources of muscle cells.

findings.statement: Askanas et al. (1976) reported that in a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, light microscopy of biopsied muscle showed multiple vacuoles filled with acid-phosphatase-positive material. Electron microscopy showed abnormal accumulation of glycogen in membrane-bound sacs (secondary lysosomes), some of which also contained dark membranous or homogeneous material. The newly grown fibers of the cultured muscle showed the same abnormalities.
quotes: Morphologically and biochemically, the newly grown fibers of the cultured muscle showed the same abnormalities as those of the biopsied muscle.

Light microscopy showed multiple vacuoles filled with acid-phosphatase-positive material; on ultrastructural examination there was abnormal accumulation of glycogen in membrane-bound sacs (secondary lysosomes), some of which also contained dark membranous of homogeneous material.

phenotypes.text: vacuolated muscle fibers with acid-phosphatase-positive material

findings.statement: Askanas et al. (1976) concluded that the reproduction of the morphologic and biochemical abnormalities in cultured muscle fibers supported the concept that adult-onset acid maltase deficiency is a biochemically distinct primary myopathy.
quotes: Cultured muscle fibers demonstrate the same morphologic and biochemical abnormalities characteristic of biopsied muscle, supporting the concept of a biochemically distinct primary myopathy in man.

relevance_reason: Measures residual acid maltase activity in late-onset AMD patients compared with infantile cases and argues that the two forms are genetically distinct.

findings.statement: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) used a sensitive fluorometric assay and found residual acid maltase activity in muscle biopsies from 15 patients with late-onset acid maltase deficiency (mean 6.91% of normal; range 2.4 to 12.2%). They did not find this activity in biopsy or autopsy muscle from 3 patients with the infantile form. Electrophoresis, kinetic characteristics, and subcellular fractionation indicated that the residual activity was lysosomal acid maltase and not a contaminating neutral maltase isozyme.
quotes: Residual acid maltase activity was found by a sensitive fluorometric assay in muscle biopsies from 15 patients with late-onset acid maltase deficiency (mean, 6.91 percent; range, 2.4 to 12.2) but not in biopsy or autopsy muscle from three patients with the infantile form.
Electrophoresis, kinetic characteristics, and subcellular fractionation indicated that the residual activity was lysosomal acid maltase and not a contaminating isozyme of neutral maltase.

findings.statement: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) found no correlation between the amount of residual acid maltase activity in muscle and either the clinical severity or the amount of glycogen accumulation in patients with late-onset acid maltase deficiency.
quotes: There was no correlation between the amount of residual acid maltase activity and the severity of the clinical picture or glycogen accumulation.

findings.statement: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) found acid maltase activity in muscle, liver, and especially leukocytes in late-onset but not infantile acid maltase deficiency. The two forms also did not occur together in the same family. From this, the authors suggested that the late-onset and infantile forms are genetically distinct.
quotes: The presence of acid maltase activity in muscle, liver, and, to a greater extent, leukocytes in late-onset but not infantile acid maltase deficiency and the failure of the two disease forms to occur in the same family suggest that they are genetically distinct.

relevance_reason: Biochemical/immunologic characterization of GAA in adult-form (late-onset) acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts versus infantile form.

findings.statement: Beratis et al. (1978) purified acid alpha-glucosidase from normal fibroblasts and from fibroblasts of a patient with the adult form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency and found that the pH optimum, Michaelis constant, electrophoretic mobility in starch, thermal denaturation at pH 4.0 and 7.0, and inhibition by turanose, alpha-methylglucoside and trehalose were the same in the mutant and normal enzyme.
quotes: Acid alpha-glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.20) was purified from normal and from adult acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts.

The pH optimum; Michaelis constant; electrophoretic mobility in starch; thermal denaturation at pH 4.0 and 7.0; and inhibition by turanose, alpha-methylglucoside and trehalose were the same in purified enzyme from normal and mutant cells.

findings.statement: Using monospecific antibodies against placental acid alpha-glucosidase, Beratis et al. (1978) found that cross-reacting material (CRM) in adult-form acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts appeared significantly reduced compared with normal cells or infantile-form cells, and that the immune complexes from adult-form cells retained enzyme activity, whereas those from infantile-form cells did not. They concluded that in the adult form the mutation causes a reduction in the amount of enzyme protein in the cells, whereas the infantile case resulted from a structural gene mutation producing a catalytically inactive, CRM-positive protein.
quotes: The amount of CRM in the adult form appeared to be significantly less than in normal cells or cells from the infantile form.
Enzyme activity was demonstrated in the immune complexes of the normal and adult acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts, but not of the infantile form.
It appears that in the adult form, the mutation causes a reduction in the amount of the enzyme protein present in the cells.

findings.statement: Beratis et al. (1978) observed competition for antibody binding sites between normal enzyme and both infantile and adult mutant enzymes. They suggested that the infantile and adult forms of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency have different molecular defects: an inactive CRM-positive protein in the infantile form and a reduced amount of enzyme protein in the adult form.
quotes: Competition for antibody binding sites was observed between normal and both types of mutant enzymes.

The findings indicate that this case of infantile acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency is the result of a structural gene mutation which causes the synthesis of a catalytically inactive (CRM-positive) enzyme protein.
